newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Buyers snub sale of Mongolia department store.
newsitem.headline: Buyers snub sale of Mongolia department store.

text.p: Mongolia failed in its second attempt to auction off its only department store on Monday when no one turned up to bid, officials of the state privatisation committee said.
Seven smaller state-owned shops were sold at the auction but the main attraction, the capital's department store, remained firmly in government hands, the officials said.
"The auction of the State Department Store was supposed to start at 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) today, but nobody came," Odgerel (Eds: one name), a committee official, told Reuters.
The 3.4 billion tugrik ($4.9 million) minimum price for the seven-story shop could have been one reason for the lack of domestic buying interest, Odgerel said.
"Perhaps nobody had so much money," she said, adding the government now had to decide whether it would try once more to auction off the store, which employs 475 people.
The department store was previously put on auction but the sale was later judged unfair and the shop re-nationalised.
No foreign investors had showed up to bid for the shop on Monday, possibly because they had not heard of the sale, said a Japanese businessman based in Mongolia.
"I learned about the auction only last week," he said. "But there was no immediate information available in detail about the store's finances."

The sale had been promoted abroad via the global Internet computer network, with an advertisement describing it as enjoying fixed assets at the beginning of September of 29.33 billion tugriks and current assets of 1.44 billion tugriks.
Store debts totalled 967.43 million tugriks, the advertisement showed.
Privatisation officials said they could not immediately explain why the department store's asking price was so low compared to its advertised assets.

The sale of retail outlets is the first step in an ambitious privatisation programme announced by Mongolia's new government, which defeated the former communist Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party in a general election earlier this year.
Mongolia began privatising state assets in 1991 shortly after a peaceful revolution the year before ended nearly 70 years of communist rule.

Officials in Ulan Bator said last year they would privatise the department store and in January selected a proposal by the Tushig Co, headed by the store's deputy director. The proposed privatisation sparked a strike and hunger strike by store workers in June.
Monday's auction enjoyed more success with sales of smaller shops, the privatisation officials said.
Seven shops were sold at prices ranging from 36.3 million tugriks to 180 million tugriks, Odgerel said.
The next state privatisation auction has been called for December 17, with nine state-owned shops to go on the block. ($1 = 700 tugriks)
